claim: Actomyosin contractility is regulated by Rho-GTP in cell migration, cytokinesis and morphogenesis in embryo development.
source: Actomyosin contractility is regulated by Rho-GTP in cell migration, cytokinesis and morphogenesis in embryo development.
evidence: This is a general statement about Rho-GTP function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: RhoGEF2 activates Rho in actomyosin contractility during cytokinesis at the base of invaginating membranes in Drosophila cellularization.
source: Whereas Rho activation by Rho-GTP exchange factor (GEF), RhoGEF2, is well known in actomyosin contractility during cytokinesis at the base of invaginating membranes in Drosophila cellularization, Rho inhibition by RhoGTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) remains to be studied.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about RhoGEF2 function in the field.

claim: GRAF is enriched at the cleavage furrow tip during actomyosin assembly and initiation of ring constriction.
source: GRAF is enriched at the cleavage furrow tip during actomyosin assembly and initiation of ring constriction.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Graf depletion shows increased Rho-GTP.
source: Graf depletion shows increased Rho-GTP, increased Myosin II and ring hyper constriction dependent upon the loss of the RhoGTPase domain.
evidence: This is supported by AnillinRBD-GFP imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: Graf depletion shows increased Myosin II.
source: Graf depletion shows increased Rho-GTP, increased Myosin II and ring hyper constriction dependent upon the loss of the RhoGTPase domain.
evidence: This is supported by Zipper and Sqh-mCherry imaging data in Figure 6.

claim: Graf depletion shows ring hyper constriction dependent upon the loss of the RhoGTPase domain.
source: Graf depletion shows increased Rho-GTP, increased Myosin II and ring hyper constriction dependent upon the loss of the RhoGTPase domain.
evidence: This is supported by ring area measurements in Figure 1 and rescue experiments with GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP in Figure 4.

claim: GRAF and RhoGEF2 are present in a balance for appropriate activation of actomyosin ring constriction.
source: GRAF and RhoGEF2 are present in a balance for appropriate activation of actomyosin ring constriction.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing suppression of phenotypes in double mutants/overexpression combinations in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: RhoGEF2 depletion suppresses the Graf hyper constriction defect.
source: RhoGEF2 depletion and abrogation of Myosin II activation in Rho kinase mutants suppress the Graf hyper constriction defect.
evidence: This is supported by ring area measurements in GrafCR57; RhoGEF2i embryos shown in Figure 8.

claim: Abrogation of Myosin II activation in Rho kinase mutants suppresses the Graf hyper constriction defect.
source: RhoGEF2 depletion and abrogation of Myosin II activation in Rho kinase mutants suppress the Graf hyper constriction defect.
evidence: This is supported by ring area measurements in GrafCR57; roki embryos shown in Figure 9.

claim: GRAF recruitment restricts Rho-GTP levels in a spatiotemporal manner for inhibiting actomyosin contractility during cellularization.
source: Therefore, GRAF recruitment restricts Rho-GTP levels in a spatiotemporal manner for inhibiting actomyosin contractility during cellularization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including GRAF localization, Rho-GTP levels, and contractility measurements.

claim: The cortical actomyosin activity is orchestrated with plasma membrane shape remodeling to generate localized forces to drive cell shape dynamics.
source: The cortical actomyosin activity is orchestrated with plasma membrane shape remodeling to generate localized forces to drive cell shape dynamics (Heer and Martin, 2017; Jodoin et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2009; Mason et al., 2013; Munjal et al., 2015; Murrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The intensity and directionality of force generated are dependent on spatiotemporal regulation of Myosin II activity.
source: The intensity and directionality of force generated are dependent on spatiotemporal regulation of Myosin II activity (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Rauzi et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myosin II activation by phosphorylation is achieved by Rho kinase.
source: Myosin II activation by phosphorylation is achieved by Rho kinase (Amano et al., 2010; Kasza et al., 2014; Levayer and Lecuit, 2012; Vasquez et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Rho-GTP activates Rho kinase.
source: Rho-GTP, a member of the small GTPases belonging to the Ras superfamily, activates Rho kinase (Prudnikova et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Rho-GTP and Rho-GDP cycling is catalyzed by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPases-activating proteins (GAPs).
source: This Rho-GTP and Rho-GDP cycling is catalyzed by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPases-activating proteins (GAPs) (Bos et al., 2007; Van Aelst and D'Souza-Schorey, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RhoGEFs lead to the production of Rho-GTP.
source: RhoGEFs lead to the production of Rho-GTP, whereas RhoGAPs promote hydrolysis of the GTP to generate Rho-GDP (Jacobs and Hall, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RhoGAPs promote hydrolysis of the GTP to generate Rho-GDP.
source: RhoGEFs lead to the production of Rho-GTP, whereas RhoGAPs promote hydrolysis of the GTP to generate Rho-GDP (Jacobs and Hall, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Drosophila embryo begins development as a syncytium.
source: The Drosophila embryo begins development as a syncytium (Foe et al., 2000; Foe and Alberts, 1983; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Transition from the syncytial to cellular blastoderm occurs at the embryo cortex in the interphase of cycle 14 by cleavage to separate each nucleus by plasma membrane boundaries in a process called cellularization.
source: Transition from the syncytial to cellular blastoderm occurs at the embryo cortex in the interphase of cycle 14 by cleavage to separate each nucleus by plasma membrane boundaries in a process called cellularization (Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993a; Sullivan and Theurkauf, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The actomyosin network assembles at the base of the furrow canal and forms a polygonal network in early cellularization.
source: The actomyosin network assembles at the base of the furrow canal and forms a polygonal network in early cellularization.
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about cellularization.

claim: The polygonal actomyosin network transforms into a contractile ring in mid cellularization.
source: This transforms into a contractile ring in mid cellularization.
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about cellularization.

claim: Ring constriction partially closes the base of the cell during late cellularization.
source: Finally, ring constriction partially closes the base of the cell during late cellularization (Kiehart, 1990; Krueger et al., 2019; Young et al., 1993; Royou et al., 2004; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993a; Xue and Sokac, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The actomyosin ring organization and constriction in cellularization are similar to conventional cytokinesis in somatic cells.
source: The actomyosin ring organization and constriction in cellularization are similar to conventional cytokinesis in somatic cells (Tram et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RhoGEF2 localizes at the furrow tip in cellularization.
source: The GTPase exchange factor, RhoGEF2, localizes at the furrow tip in cellularization, and its depletion results in inhibition of ring constriction in cellularization (Padash Barmchi et al., 2005; Grosshans et al., 2005; Wenzl et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RhoGEF2 depletion results in inhibition of ring constriction in cellularization.
source: The GTPase exchange factor, RhoGEF2, localizes at the furrow tip in cellularization, and its depletion results in inhibition of ring constriction in cellularization (Padash Barmchi et al., 2005; Grosshans et al., 2005; Wenzl et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 8.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the catalytic domain of RhoGEF2 in the assembly phase of Myosin II leads to increased Myosin II recruitment, resulting in premature and enhanced constriction.
source: Optogenetic activation of the catalytic domain of RhoGEF2 in the assembly phase of Myosin II leads to increased Myosin II recruitment, resulting in premature and enhanced constriction (Krueger et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of RhoGEF2 and activated Rho1 mutant Rho1V14 results in contracted S2 cell morphology.
source: Moreover, overexpression of RhoGEF2 and activated Rho1 mutant Rho1V14 results in contracted S2 cell morphology (Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Microinjection of Rho1 inhibitor, C3 exoenzyme, and dominant negative N19Rho alters the actin cytoskeleton and disrupts cellularization.
source: On the other hand, microinjection of Rho1 inhibitor, C3 exoenzyme, and dominant negative N19Rho alters the actin cytoskeleton and disrupts cellularization (Crawford et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Rok and Drak mutant embryos show impaired actomyosin contractility due to reduced Myosin II phosphorylation.
source: Further, Rok and Drak mutant embryos and addition of a pharmacological inhibitor of Rok, Y-27632, show impaired actomyosin contractility due to reduced Myosin II phosphorylation (Chougule et al., 2016; Krajcovic and Minden, 2012; Xue and Sokac, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phospho-deficient mutants of the light chain of Myosin II, Squash, show loss of contractility during cellularization.
source: Phospho-deficient mutants of the light chain of Myosin II, Squash, also show loss of contractility during cellularization (Xue and Sokac, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Depletion of RhoGAPs, RGA3 and RGA4 in the Caenorhabditis elegans embryo leads to enhanced contractility of the anterior cortex due to increased recruitment of Myosin II.
source: Depletion of RhoGAPs, RGA3 and RGA4 in the Caenorhabditis elegans embryo leads to enhanced contractility of the anterior cortex due to increased recruitment of Myosin II (Regev et al., 2017; Schmutz et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CGAP plays a role in inhibiting apical constriction in gastrulation.
source: CGAP, a RhoGAP identified in Drosophila embryos, plays a role in inhibiting apical constriction in gastrulation (Mason et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CGAP mutant embryos show increased constriction of actomyosin rings in cellularization.
source: CGAP mutant embryos also show increased constriction of actomyosin rings in cellularization (Mason et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The hexagonal phase of actomyosin organization has been shown to be resilient to activation by Myosin II recruitment.
source: The hexagonal phase of actomyosin organization has been shown to be resilient to activation by Myosin II recruitment, and RhoGAPs may function at this stage to inhibit ring constriction (Krueger et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GRAF is a multidomain protein containing a BAR, PH, RhoGAP and SH3 domain.
source: GRAF is a multidomain protein containing a BAR, PH, RhoGAP and SH3 domain (Lundmark et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GRAF was originally identified as a binding partner of the C-terminal domain of focal adhesion kinase.
source: GRAF was originally identified as a binding partner of the C-terminal domain of focal adhesion kinase (Hildebrand et al., 1996; Taylor et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The BAR and PH domains are important for the recruitment of GRAF to the membrane.
source: The BAR and PH domains are important for the recruitment of GRAF to the membrane, and RhoGAP domain specifically regulates the GTPase activity of RhoA (Doherty and Lundmark, 2009; Doherty et al., 2011; Eberth et al., 2009; Holst et al., 2017; Lundmark et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The RhoGAP domain of GRAF specifically regulates the GTPase activity of RhoA.
source: The BAR and PH domains are important for the recruitment of GRAF to the membrane, and RhoGAP domain specifically regulates the GTPase activity of RhoA (Doherty and Lundmark, 2009; Doherty et al., 2011; Eberth et al., 2009; Holst et al., 2017; Lundmark et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GRAF-deficient smooth muscle cells in mice and Xenopus embryo extracts have increased Rho-GTP levels.
source: GRAF-deficient smooth muscle cells in mice and Xenopus embryo extracts have increased Rho-GTP levels (Bai et al., 2013; Doherty et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GRAF loss leads to depletion of epithelial markers and transition to mesenchymal markers, giving rise to enhanced migratory ability.
source: GRAF loss leads to depletion of epithelial markers and transition to mesenchymal markers, giving rise to enhanced migratory ability (Regev et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The GRAF protein domain organization is conserved across multicellular organisms including C. elegans, Drosophila, Xenopus, chick, zebrafish and humans.
source: This domain organization is conserved across the multicellular organisms, C. elegans, Drosophila, Xenopus, chick, zebrafish and humans (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; Contrino et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Grafi expressing embryos showed 94% lethality at 24 hr.
source: F1 females containing the Gal4 and shRNA gave embryos that were lethal at 24 hr (Grafi 94% were lethal, n = 532 embryos, and Graf2i 98% were lethal, n = 540 embryos).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: Graf2i expressing embryos showed 98% lethality at 24 hr.
source: F1 females containing the Gal4 and shRNA gave embryos that were lethal at 24 hr (Grafi 94% were lethal, n = 532 embryos, and Graf2i 98% were lethal, n = 540 embryos).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: During early stages of cellularization (furrow length 3–6 μm), the F-actin network at the basal part of furrow was organized as a polygonal array.
source: During early stages of cellularization (furrow length 3–6 μm), the F-actin network at the basal part of furrow was organized as a polygonal array (white arrowheads, Figure 1C; He et al., 2016; Xue and Sokac, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Grafi and Graf2i expressing embryos did not show the polygonal F-actin organization in early stages.
source: Grafi and Graf2i expressing embryos did not show the polygonal F-actin organization in early stages (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In Grafi embryos, the furrow tips contained wavy edges with a loss of contact between adjacent furrow tips.
source: In Grafi embryos, the furrow tips contained wavy edges with a loss of contact between adjacent furrow tips (white arrowheads, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was enhanced constriction in mid and late stages of cellularization in Grafi embryos.
source: There was enhanced constriction in mid and late stages of cellularization (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nuclei had a bottleneck appearance in Grafi embryos possibly due to premature constriction and squeezing of nuclei in mid cellularization.
source: The nuclei had a bottleneck appearance in Grafi embryos possibly due to premature constriction and squeezing of nuclei in mid cellularization (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Quantification of the area of the contractile rings showed a significant decrease in Grafi as compared to controls in early, mid and late cellularization.
source: Quantification of the area of the contractile rings showed a significant decrease in Grafi as compared to controls in early, mid and late cellularization (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GrafCR57 homozygous adult females gave embryos with 71% lethality at 24 hr.
source: GrafCR57/GrafCR57 homozygous adult females gave embryos with 71% lethality at 24 hr (n = 336).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: GrafCR57 embryos did not show polygonal F-actin architecture in early cellularization.
source: Like the Grafi expressing embryos, GrafCR57 embryos obtained from homozygous GrafCR57/GrafCR57 parents did not show polygonal F-actin architecture in early cellularization.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GrafCR57 embryos showed premature ring formation in early cellularization and enhanced ring constriction in mid and late cellularization.
source: They showed premature ring formation in early cellularization and enhanced ring constriction in mid and late cellularization (white arrowheads, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Quantification of ring area of GrafCR57 embryos in cellularization showed a significant decrease in early, mid and late stages as compared to controls.
source: Quantification of ring area of GrafCR57 embryos in cellularization showed a significant decrease in early, mid and late stages as compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The ring constriction defects were enhanced in GrafCR57 as compared to Grafi embryos.
source: The ring constriction defects were enhanced in GrafCR57 as compared to Grafi embryos (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GrafCR57 embryos had bottleneck-shaped nuclei in cellularization.
source: GrafCR57 embryos also had bottleneck-shaped nuclei in cellularization (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of polygonal F-actin organization and premature ring constriction at the furrow tip is also seen in embryos depleted of Bottleneck in cellularization.
source: Loss of polygonal F-actin organization and premature ring constriction at the furrow tip is also seen in embryos depleted of Bottleneck, a phospholipid-binding and actin-organizing protein, in cellularization (Krueger et al., 2019; Reversi et al., 2014; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GRAF antibody stained the furrow tip basal to Dlg throughout cellularization.
source: GRAF antibody stained the furrow tip basal to Dlg throughout cellularization (yellow arrowhead, sagittal section, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The grazing section across the furrow tip showed an enrichment of GRAF recruitment at edges and a reduction at vertices in early cellularization.
source: The grazing section across the furrow tip showed an enrichment of GRAF recruitment at edges (white arrowhead, Figure 2A) and a reduction at vertices in early cellularization (yellow arrowhead, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GRAF antibody staining increased at regions corresponding to tight edges in the Dlg staining during mid cellularization.
source: GRAF antibody staining increased at regions corresponding to tight edges in the Dlg staining during mid cellularization and was occasionally absent from curved regions (yellow arrowhead, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GRAF antibody staining was weakly present in rings in late cellularization.
source: GRAF antibody staining was weakly present in rings in late cellularization (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: The GRAF staining was lost in 100% GrafCR57 embryos as compared to controls.
source: The GRAF staining was lost in 100% GrafCR57 embryos as compared to controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Quantification of the cortex to cytosol fluorescence showed a significant reduction in intensity in GrafCR57 as compared to controls.
source: Quantification of the cortex to cytosol fluorescence showed a significant reduction in intensity as compared to controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Grafi expressing embryos showed a depletion in GRAF antibody staining in 64% of the embryos.
source: Grafi expressing embryos showed a depletion in GRAF antibody staining in 64% of the embryos, and the cortex to cytosol intensity was significantly decreased as compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The greater loss of GRAF in GrafCR57 correlated with more severe defects in ring constriction seen in GrafCR57 as compared to Grafi.
source: The greater loss of GRAF in GrafCR57 also correlated with more severe defects in ring constriction seen in GrafCR57 as compared to Grafi (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing GRAF levels and ring constriction phenotypes.

claim: GrafCR57 led to a complete loss of function for Graf.
source: GrafCR57 therefore led to a complete loss of function, and Grafi led to a partial loss-of-function phenotype for Graf.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the severity of phenotypes and GRAF protein levels.

claim: Grafi led to a partial loss-of-function phenotype for Graf.
source: GrafCR57 therefore led to a complete loss of function, and Grafi led to a partial loss-of-function phenotype for Graf.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the severity of phenotypes and GRAF protein levels.

claim: GRAF-GFP was already present at edges in early cellularization during the Myosin II assembly phase when Sqh-mCherry was seen in foci.
source: GRAF-GFP was already present at edges in early cellularization during the Myosin II assembly phase when Sqh-mCherry was seen in foci.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: GRAF-GFP increased further along with Sqh-mCherry at the start of mid cellularization.
source: GRAF-GFP increased further along with Sqh-mCherry at the start of mid cellularization.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: GRAF-GFP was lost from the furrow in late cellularization when Sqh-mCherry was present in the constricted ring.
source: GRAF-GFP was lost from the furrow in late cellularization when Sqh-mCherry was present in the constricted ring (Figure 2D, E, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2D, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: GrafCR57 embryos showed an approximately fourfold increase in maximum displacement at 70 s as compared to controls in both early and mid cellularization.
source: GrafCR57 embryos showed an approximately fourfold increase in maximum displacement at 70 s as compared to controls in both early and mid cellularization (Figure 3C, G).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation data shown in Figure 3C, G.

claim: Initial recoil velocities of the edges after ablations were increased by approximately twofold in GrafCR57 embryos in early and mid stages of cellularization as compared to controls.
source: Similarly, initial recoil velocities of the edges after ablations were increased by approximately twofold in GrafCR57 embryos in early and mid stages of cellularization as compared to controls (Figure 3D, H).
evidence: This is supported by laser ablation data shown in Figure 3D, H.

claim: The increased displacement and recoil velocity of the ring edges suggest that the actomyosin network in GrafCR57 has increased contractility.
source: This increased displacement and recoil velocity of the ring edges suggest that the actomyosin network in GrafCR57 has increased contractility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the laser ablation measurements.

claim: AnillinRBD-GFP was present as foci that colocalized with Sqh-mCherry in early cellularization during the assembly of the actomyosin complex at the furrow tip.
source: AnillinRBD-GFP was present as foci that colocalized with Sqh-mCherry in early cellularization during the assembly of the actomyosin complex at the furrow tip.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AnillinRBD-GFP was present along with Sqh-mCherry at the contractile ring in mid and late cellularization.
source: AnillinRBD-GFP was present along with Sqh-mCherry at the contractile ring in mid and late cellularization in images (Figure 4A, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A and Video 4.

claim: Anillin-RBD fluorescence increased from early to mid stages and decreased in late stages of cellularization in control embryos.
source: Anillin-RBD fluorescence increased from early to mid stages and decreased in late stages of cellularization in control embryos (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AnillinRBD-GFP and Sqh-mCherry signal was more spread during early and mid stages of cellularization in GrafCR57 embryos compared to sharp colocalization peaks in control.
source: AnillinRBD-GFP and Sqh-mCherry signal was more spread during early and mid stages of cellularization in GrafCR57 embryos compared to sharp colocalization peaks in control (Figure 4C, D, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4C, D and Video 4.

claim: The increase in Rho-GTP in early and mid stages of cellularization correlated with hyper contractility in GrafCR57 embryos.
source: This increase in Rho-GTP in early and mid stages of cellularization correlated with hyper contractility in GrafCR57 embryos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the AnillinRBD-GFP data and contractility measurements.

claim: GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP recruited to the furrow until mid cellularization and was lost from the furrow in late cellularization similar to GRAF-GFP.
source: Similar to GRAF-GFP, GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP recruited to the furrow until mid cellularization and was lost from the furrow in late cellularization similar to GRAF-GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP appeared in punctae in early cellularization, leading to higher relative fluorescence as compared to GRAF-GFP in early cellularization.
source: However, GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP appeared in punctae in early cellularization, leading to higher relative fluorescence as compared to GRAF-GFP in early cellularization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The ring area in GrafCR57 embryos was significantly lower than controls during cellularization.
source: The ring area in GrafCR57 embryos was significantly lower than controls during cellularization (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: The hyper constriction phenotype in GrafCR57 was suppressed in GrafCR57; GRAF-GFP embryos.
source: This hyper constriction phenotype in GrafCR57 was suppressed in GrafCR57; GRAF-GFP embryos.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: GrafCR57; GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP embryos showed hyper constriction of rings similar to GrafCR57.
source: GrafCR57; GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP embryos, on the other hand, showed hyper constriction of rings similar to GrafCR57 (Figure 4F, G, Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F, G and Videos 5 and 6.

claim: The full-length GRAF-GFP suppressed the constriction defect of GrafCR57.
source: Thus, the full-length GRAF-GFP suppressed the constriction defect of GrafCR57.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment data.

claim: The RhoGAP domain in GRAF protein was necessary for restricting ring constriction during cellularization.
source: The RhoGAP domain in GRAF protein was necessary for restricting ring constriction during cellularization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GRAFΔRhoGAP-GFP rescue experiment.

claim: GRAF-OE embryos showed a significant increase in GRAF antibody staining as compared to controls.
source: GRAF-OE embryos showed a significant increase in GRAF antibody staining as compared to controls (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: The ring area was significantly larger in GRAF-OE as compared to controls from early stages of cellularization.
source: We found that the ring area was significantly larger in GRAF-OE as compared to controls from early stages of cellularization (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5D, E.

claim: GRAF overexpression leads to inhibition of ring constriction during cellularization.
source: These data show that GRAF overexpression leads to inhibition of ring constriction during cellularization consistent with increased RhoGTPase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GRAF-OE data.

claim: The Zipper fluorescence at the furrow tip relative to the cytoplasm was significantly increased in GrafCR57 throughout cellularization as compared to control embryos.
source: We found that the Zipper fluorescence at the furrow tip relative to the cytoplasm was significantly increased in GrafCR57 throughout cellularization as compared to control embryos (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Zipper foci in GrafCR57 appeared larger than controls in early cellularization.
source: Zipper foci in GrafCR57 appeared larger than controls in early cellularization, and Zipper was also enriched in between adjacent rings in mid cellularization (white arrowheads, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Zipper was enriched in between adjacent rings in mid cellularization in GrafCR57.
source: Zipper foci in GrafCR57 appeared larger than controls in early cellularization, and Zipper was also enriched in between adjacent rings in mid cellularization (white arrowheads, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dynamics of furrow length increase in the slow and fast phase in GRAF-OE were similar to controls during cellularization.
source: The dynamics of furrow length increase in the slow and fast phase in GRAF-OE were similar to controls during cellularization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Figard et al., 2013; He et al., 2016; Lecuit and Wieschaus, 2000; Merrill et al., 1988; Royou et al., 2004; Warn and Magrath, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The slow phase in GrafCR57 was extended and the fast phase started at a later time point.
source: In contrast, the slow phase in GrafCR57 was extended and the fast phase started at a later time point (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GRAF-OE embryos showed a delay in Sqh-mCherry peak as compared to controls.
source: GRAF-OE embryos showed a delay in Sqh-mCherry peak as compared to controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GrafCR57 showed a sustained Sqh-mCherry fluorescence throughout cellularization, and it remained significantly higher at later stages of cellularization.
source: GrafCR57, on the other hand, showed a sustained Sqh-mCherry fluorescence throughout cellularization, and it remained significantly higher at later stages of cellularization (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Videos 5 and 7).
